title: The first screen of a support inbox
metaTitle: Support inbox UX: the first screen
excerpt: Open a support inbox on the next conversation the agent should handle, with the customer's words, the wait, and one action that sends or assigns. Charts and tours can wait.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table, a grid of doors when the job is the next conversation.
caption: The icons are many. The next conversation is one. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a support inbox show?
faqs.answer: The next conversation: who it is, what they last said, how long they have waited, and any promise already made. The main action is reply or assign, depending on the role, not both at equal strength. The rest of the queue can sit quietly beside that thread.

faqs.question: What context belongs next to the reply?
faqs.answer: The few facts that stop a wrong answer, such as plan, order, and the last internal note, each with a source. The whole customer record can open on demand. Internal notes must be visually distinct from words that will be sent to the customer.

faqs.question: How should two agents in one thread be handled?
faqs.answer: Show that someone else is replying, and keep a second send behind a confirmation or a read-only state. Opening a row should not silently assign it unless the screen says that is the rule. Snoozed conversations need a visible home so they can come back.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A support inbox ux should open on the next conversation an agent is meant to handle, with enough context to answer and one action that sends or assigns. A tour of the help desk is the wrong object. The object is the conversation.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people often leave a web page in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear in the first 10. An agent under a queue is less patient than that. If the first screen is a dashboard of averages, they will alt-tab to the thread that actually needs a reply.

## The object is the next conversation

Name whose turn it is. "Yours, 6 waiting." Then show the conversation that should be answered first, not a mosaic of every queue in the company. The subject or the customer's first line, the customer's name, how long they have been waiting, and whether anyone has already promised them something. Those four facts decide the next minute. A satisfaction score and a weekly volume chart do not.

Put the one action on that conversation. Reply, or assign, or take it. If the agent's job is to answer, the reply box is the action, already focused, with the customer's last message above it. If the agent's job is to route, the action is assign, and a reply box is a trap. Do not give both equal weight and hope the role sorts it out. The first screen can know the role.

Show the promise you have already made. If the plan says first response in an hour, and this customer has waited forty minutes, say that next to the name. A colored dot is not the promise. The words are. Agents should not have to decode a legend while someone is waiting.

Leave the rest of the queue visible and quiet, as a list under or beside the open conversation. The agent needs to know the next three exist. They do not need those three to shout. Order the list by the rule you are willing to defend: oldest unanswered, or a promised time that is about to lapse, or a VIP flag the company actually honors. If two rules conflict, write the order down on the screen in one line. "Oldest unanswered first. Promised times float to the top."

## Context that fits in the margin

The conversation is the object. The context is what stops a wrong answer. Order, plan, last purchase, and the two previous tickets, if they exist. Put them in a column the agent can scan, not in a scavenger hunt of tabs. Leadly and Got Next are public examples of product UI that keeps one job on the screen. A support inbox should be that disciplined. Trade Moai is a reminder that scanability is the layout, not a feature you add later.

Each context row needs a source and a freshness. "Plan: Standard, from billing, today." A row that might be yesterday's cache should say so. Agents will quote this margin to the customer. If it is stale, the reply will be wrong, and the inbox will get the blame.

Do not dump the entire customer record into the margin. A shipping address matters when the ticket is about a delivery. It is noise when the ticket is about a receipt. Start with the few fields that are useful on most replies, and let the agent open the rest. The first screen's job is the next true sentence, not a biography.

Internal notes from the last agent belong above the reply box, visually distinct from the customer's words. "Promised a replacement, waiting on the warehouse." If that note is easy to miss, the next agent will promise something else. Notes are part of the object. Style them so they cannot be confused with a message that will be sent.

## What does not belong above the reply

A product tour, a weekly stats page, a leaderboard of who closed the most tickets, a changelog, a prompt to install a mobile app. Those can exist. They cannot occupy the first viewport of someone whose job is the next conversation. The same rule covers motivational empty states. If the queue is clear, say "Nothing waiting on you," and show where new conversations will appear. Do not make them dismiss a celebration before they can see that the queue is empty.

Macros and saved replies are tools, not the screen. Offer them inside the reply, as a short list of this team's actual replies, with names a new agent can understand. "Where is my order." "Refund approved." A picker of eighty snippets with codes for titles is a second product. Keep the frequent few close. Search can find the rest, which is a later concern, not the first screen's.

Channel chrome should be quiet. Email, chat, and a social message can share one thread if that is how your team works, and the channel should be a label, not a different app. The agent should see that a reply will go by email before they hit send. Say the destination in the button if it is ambiguous. "Send email to jess@…" is a promise. "Submit" is not.

## Assignment, collision, and the second agent

Say when someone else is already in the conversation. "Sam is replying." Let the second agent read, and hold their send behind a confirmation, or make the reply box read-only until they take it over. Two sends, two promises, one customer. The first screen has to prevent that without hiding the thread. Hidden threads feel like lost mail. A banner on a visible thread feels like the product is paying attention.

Taking a conversation should be explicit when the queue is shared. Opening a row can mark it as being read. It should not silently assign it forever. Say the rule near the list. "Opening does not assign. Take it if it is yours to finish." Founders often want the opposite rule. Either is fine if it is written on the screen. A silent rule will be discovered as a bug by every new hire.

Snooze and waiting-on-customer are statuses, not trash. They need a visible home so a conversation can return when the timer ends or the customer writes back. If snoozed items vanish, agents will use the inbox as a graveyard of browser tabs instead. Show the count of snoozed items. Do not show them mixed into the active list without a label.

## The customer's clock, not the agent's vanity

Waiting time should be the customer's wait, not the time since the agent last touched the ticket. Those are different clocks, and mixing them makes a recently poked, still-unanswered thread look healthy. Put the customer wait on the row. Put "last internal touch" in the margin if the team needs it for coaching. Coaching is not the first screen's job. Answering is.

If you show a clock, show the one that matches the promise you sell. A 24-hour first-response promise, measured in business hours, should say "business hours" on the row. A raw elapsed timer that runs over the weekend will train agents to panic on Monday and to ignore the promise the rest of the week. The number on the screen becomes the culture. Choose it on purpose.

A breach that has already happened should change the sentence, not only the color. "First response was due 20 minutes ago." The next action is still to reply. The sentence explains why this row is above the others. Color can agree with the sentence. Color cannot replace it.

## Review a live minute

Count the clicks between arrival and a cursor in the reply. On a Hanabi-built inbox the aim is one: the conversation is already open, the box is already focused, the context is already in the margin. A second click to dismiss a tip, and a third to choose a queue, means the first screen is still introducing itself. The agent already knows why they opened it.

Watch one agent start their day. In the first ten seconds they should be able to say which conversation is next, why it is next, and what will happen if they hit the main button. If they cannot, the screen is still a tour of your features.

Then watch a collision, an empty queue, and a thread with a promise in the notes. Each needs a sentence. The failure modes, a send that did not go, an attachment the customer never got, belong beside this screen, not as an afterthought. [Errors in a support inbox](/blog/errors-in-a-support-inbox) is the next piece, because a reply that fails must say whether the customer saw it.

Hanabi designs this first screen in Figma with a real thread, not lorem lines, then builds it in Next.js, React, and TypeScript. Tailwind holds the hierarchy: the customer's words, then the reply, then the margin. Motion can mark a sent message. It should not animate the queue into place while someone is waiting. Prisma and PostgreSQL are a natural place for the conversation, the assignment, and the note, so two agents are not reading two different truths.

If your agents still hunt for the next conversation under a layer of charts, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring a redacted thread and the rule you wish the queue obeyed. The work should name the object and the one action.
